events.title: Colony of Fiji
hints: A paramount chief and his peers ceded sovereignty to Queen Victoria in 1874.
Settler debts and instability had preceded the cession.
Sugar plantations became the colony's backbone.
events.summary: In October 1874 Cakobau and other chiefs signed the Deed of Cession, making Fiji a British Crown colony. The colonial government protected most land for indigenous owners but built an economy around sugar plantations, with indentured labour from India, until independence in 1970.

events.title: Indian indenture system
hints: Ships called the Leonidas brought workers from South Asia from 1879.
About sixty thousand people were contracted for five years.
The system ended in 1916 after campaigns by reformers.
events.summary: Between 1879 and 1916 about 61,000 Indian labourers, called girmitiyas after the word 'agreement', were shipped to work on sugar plantations under five-year contracts. Conditions were often harsh, with high suicide rates and abuses, and most chose to stay, creating a large Indo-Fijian community.

events.title: Blackbirding and the Pacific labour trade
hints: Islanders from other groups were tricked or kidnapped onto ships to work on plantations.
A cotton boom in the 1860s created a demand for labour.
Recruitment of Pacific Islanders continued until 1911.
events.summary: From 1864 to 1911 tens of thousands of Pacific Islanders, mainly from Melanesia, were recruited, often through deception or kidnapping, to work on plantations in the colony, first for cotton and later sugar and copra. Many died of disease and overwork.

events.title: Tongan hegemony over the former domains of the Tui Fiti
hints: Tongan voyaging kings extended their reach westward across the Pacific from about 950 and peaked between 1200 and 1500.
The empire grew to include much of the former domains of a rival paramount chief.
Linguistic and archaeological evidence shows Tongan influence on the island group of Rotuma and elsewhere in this archipelago.
events.summary: At its height, from about 1200 to 1500, the Tuʻi Tonga Empire extended over much of the former domains of the Tui Fiti, and tribute was due to the Tuʻi Tonga. Modern archaeology, anthropology and linguistics confirm widespread Tongan influence in Fiji, including on Rotuma. Scholars debate whether to call this an empire or a maritime chiefdom, and the dates are approximate.
